top_choice_rationale: P003 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) combines a field-creating framework for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy with about three decades of replication, extension and challenge. Its credit structure is concentrated and can be described, and the Besley-Persson state-capacity and political-selection strand is separable from the constitutions-and-electoral-rules strand, so the trio is defensible. Its main weakness is identification: the cross-country evidence has endogenous institutional adoption, so the citation should say 'formal and empirically testable' and not claim causal settlement. I treat proximity to the 2024 prize as a timing consideration, not a scientific one. P001 (Chetty, Hendren, Friedman) is a close second. It has the best directly checkable identification and a tight trio, but a short record of roughly 2014 to 2022 and an open Katz question. The Kiyotaki-Moore pair in P002 attributes cleanly and is mature, but it overlaps with the financial-frictions agenda already recognised in 2022 and its aggregate evidence is mostly indirect or calibrated. P004 is influential, but a three-name cut from an eight-name cumulative field cannot be defended on a principled criterion. A prize in a year with several defensible proposals is preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley. I disclose an institutional overlap at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), who are fellow members and not candidates. Persson's IIES association is general knowledge and not established by my profile. As an empirical labour economist I may weigh identification more heavily than a theorist would. This is a disclosure only, not a recusal.
